newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China holds key to HK's international future - study.
newsitem.headline: China holds key to HK's international future - study.

text.p: Hong Kong's continued success as an international financial centre (IFC) depended almost entirely upon China, a new study released on Tuesday concluded.

Six criteria were crucial for Hong Kong's economic future, Y.C. Jao of the University of Hong Kong wrote in one of seven papers released at Tuesday's launch of a major new study of Hong Kong's economy.
"Hong Kong as International Financial Centre: Evolution, Prospects and Policies" said the six criteria were:
* whether there will be smooth transition to Chinese rule
* whether China will strictly observe its commitments under the Joint Declaration and Basic Law, and accord to Hong Kong a high degree of autonomy
* whether China will continue its market-oriented economic reform and open-door policies
* whether cross-Strait relations can stabilize without degenerating into military showdown
* whether China can maintain stable external relations with the major industrial powers, especially the U.S.
* whether Hong Kong itself will preserve the favourable internal factors responsible for its past success

"Our judgment is that these premises probably can hold, though not in an ideal manner. Moreover, only the last premise is within the control of Hong Kong, whereas China is involved in all the rest," Jao wrote.
"China therefore has a heavy responsibility for Hong Kong's future prospects as an IFC."

Even if these six premises hold, Hong Kong still confronts increasing competition from other centes in the Asia-Pacific region including established centres such as Tokyo and Singapore as well as emerging centres such as Shanghai, Taipei and Sydney.

Singapore is considered the greatest threat. Using 30 variables, Hong Kong still retains a lead but "the edge is so small that Singapore can quite easily overtake Hong Kong, espeically if the 1997 transition is not managed well."
Concrete suggestions to enhance competitiveness included:
* raising the ratio of the 17-20 age group receiving tertiary education to 30 percent from the current 18 percent within the decade

* expedite the Real Time Gross Settlement system allowing for immediate settlement of transactions in the Hong Kong money market, the Mandatory Provident Fund designed to ensure all citizens are protected for retirement, and the mortgage corporation

* exploit the Chinese connection not only by maintaining Hong Kong's present position as the leading offshore centre for syndication and capital-raising but also, eventually, as the leading centre for reinsurance and trading in Chinese yuan. Also, strengthen links with foreign financial markets, including linking up payments systems with those in China and the U.S.
